newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Recovery seen for Australian meat - ABARE.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Recovery seen for Australian meat - ABARE.

text.p: Australia's exports of beef are forecast to rise in 1997/98 (June 30) after a sustained recovery in cattle prices toward the end of 1997, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said in papers to be presented at its Outlook conference here this week.
Cattle saleyard prices are forecast to rise to 174 cents a kg in 1997/98 from 155 cents a kg in 1996/97 and are forecast to colntinue to increase to 250 cents a kg in year 2001/02.

Despite continuing competition from the United States in Australia's key beef export markets, growth in Asian beef demand is expected to underpin Australian cattle saleyard prices over the medium-term, ABARE said.

Short-term prospects also remain sound for sheep meat, it said. Australian beef and veal exports are forecast to rise to A$2.4 billion in 1997/98 from A$2.1 billion in 1996/97. The forecast for 1996/97 is steady with ABARE's December forecast.
The value of beef and veal exports in 1995/96 amounted to A$2.4 billion, said ABARE, the Australian government's main commodities forecaster.
Beef and veal exports in volume terms are forecast at 755,000 tonnes for 1997/98, up from 728,000 tonnes in 1996/97.

Despite relatively low returns for beef, improved seasonal conditions in the major cattle producing regions of New South Wales and Queensland are expected to lead to producers increasing their cattle numbers in 1996/97, ABARE said.
Cattle numbers are projected to increase by about four percent over the medium-term to about 28.5 million head by March 2002, it said.
Australia's exports of live cattle are also forecast to continue to rise, to 790,000 head in 1997/98 from a forecast 750,000 head in 1996/97.
The 1996/97 forecast is steady with ABARE's December forecast.
Live cattle exports in 1995/96 amounted to 628,000 head after jumping from 396,000 head the year before.
A key factor in change of herd size will be profitability of beef against alternative enterprises, ABARE said.
For mixed livestock producers, expected changes in the relative prices of wool and beef was likely to lead to a shift toward beef between 1997 and year 2000, it said.
However, toward the end of the projection periods in year 2001/02, when the wool stockpile is eliminated, wool prices are forecast to rise and to favour wool production, ABARE said.

Continued high prices for sheep meat, supported by significant export opportunities, are expected to lead to further expansion of the Australian sheep meat industry in 1997/98 and in 1998/99, ABARE said.
But improvements in competing enterprises such as wool and beef, together with renewed export competition from New Zealand, are expected to constrain growth in lamb production, it said.
Saleyard prices for lamb are forecast to decline in 1997/98 by six cents a kg to average 190 cents a kg largely because of increased production.
Saleyard prices for sheep are projected to remain steady in 1997/98 on 65 cents a kg nominal.
Production of mutton is projected to dip to 299,000 tonnes in 1997/98 from a forecast 305,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
Production in 1995/96 amounted to 295,000 tonnes.
Lamb production in 1997/98 is forecast to rise to 283,000 tonnes from 272,000 tonnes in 1995/96.
Exports of mutton are forecast to remain virtually steady in 1997/98 at 146,000 tonnes against 145,000 tonnes in 1996/97.
Exports of lamb in 1997/98 are forecast at 63,000 tonnes, up from 57,000 tonnes the year before.
Australian live sheep exports in 1997/98 are forecast at 5.5 million head, up from 5.3 million in 1996/97. Exports in year 2001/02 are forecast at 6.0 million head.
